title: Adding a new regex module (compatible with re)

messages.content: I'm looking into BPO-2636 regarding the proposed new regex module. It's been a long-standing issue for CPython. I've started by cloning the repo and examining the provided patches in Lib/regex.py. I'm seeing some inconsistencies with the existing re module API when running test_regex.py. Specifically, the flags handling in re.compile seems to be slightly off in the new implementation.

Thanks for picking this up. The compatibility with the re module is indeed the biggest hurdle. When you mention the flags, are you seeing issues with Unicode-related flags like re.UNICODE, or is it more generic, like re.IGNORECASE? Check the internal flags mapping in Modules/_regex.c; it's possible the bitwise operations there don't align perfectly with the standard re module's expectations.

Good catch. I dove into Modules/_regex.c and it seems the mapping for re.VERBOSE isn't being parsed correctly when passed through the re.compile interface. The underlying C code is expecting different constants than what the high-level Python API is sending. I'm going to attempt a patch to align these constants with Lib/re.py.

Be careful with that, as changing the constants in Modules/_regex.c could break compatibility with the standalone 'regex' package users might already have installed. Perhaps introduce a mapping layer or a compatibility helper function inside Lib/regex.py instead of modifying the core C constants directly? Let's check how Modules/_regex.c interacts with the PyObject representation of these flags.

That makes sense. I've implemented a translation dictionary in Lib/regex.py that maps the standard re flags to the internal _regex flags before calling the C extension functions. Now I'm getting an 'AttributeError: module _regex has no attribute __flags__' in some edge cases. It seems I need to expose these more explicitly.

Ah, the internal module needs to explicitly expose these constants. You should look at the ModuleDef in Modules/_regex.c. You likely need to add a module definition entry for the flags or ensure PyModule_AddIntConstant is called during the module initialization phase. Let me know if you need the specific snippet for the module init function.

I've added the missing constants using PyModule_AddIntConstant in the init_regex function in Modules/_regex.c. Re-running the test suite, I'm now getting a segfault in test_regex.py when calling findall with a zero-length match. It looks like it's happening in the character class scanning logic.

That sounds like a classic buffer overrun or pointer mismanagement in the scanning logic. Check the internal loop within Modules/_regex.c that handles empty string matches. Are you correctly advancing the pointer? Look specifically at the 'match_context' struct and how it handles 'pos' vs 'endpos' when the match length is zero.

I found it! In Modules/_regex.c, I wasn't checking if the input string pointer had reached the end before attempting to increment it during a zero-length match iteration. I've added a bounds check. Now the segfault is gone, but I have a regression in TestRegex.test_empty_string_match.

Interesting. Maybe the bounds check is being too aggressive? If you're preventing the increment for a zero-length match, you might be trapping the scanner in an infinite loop. Try wrapping the increment logic with an 'if (match_len > 0)' check instead of a global bounds check.

Good call. I updated the loop condition in Modules/_regex.c. The infinite loop is resolved and the test now passes. However, I'm noticing that the performance on large inputs is slightly worse than the original re module. It feels like the caching mechanism for compiled patterns isn't as efficient.

The caching in the original re module uses a simple LRU dictionary. Compare Lib/re.py's '_compile' function with your implementation in Lib/regex.py. Are you using functools.lru_cache, or a manual dictionary? Using lru_cache might be the cleanest way to improve this without adding complexity.

I switched to using functools.lru_cache for pattern compilation in Lib/regex.py and it definitely improved the speed of repeated calls. Now I'm trying to verify compatibility with the 're' module's pattern objects. I need to make sure isinstance(pattern, re.Pattern) works.

To get isinstance(pattern, re.Pattern) working, you may need to register your new RegexObject class as a virtual subclass of re.Pattern using the ABCMeta mechanism. Have you imported 'abc' and tried 're.Pattern.register(RegexObject)' in your module initialization?

That works perfectly! My RegexObject now passes the isinstance check. I'm currently running the full suite of Lib/test/test_re.py, passing it through my new module to ensure there are no breaking changes. It's taking a while, but so far so good.

That's excellent news. Make sure to also run the tests specifically designed for the new functionality (the ones provided in the issue attachment). Are there any specific features like 'atomic grouping' or 'possessive quantifiers' that are showing unexpected behavior in the new test suite?

Actually, atomic grouping is failing on nested expressions. It seems the stack handling in Modules/_regex.c doesn't correctly track nested state depths. I'm tracking the stack push/pop operations now. It looks like a simple state variable underflow.

Check your depth counter logic. If it's a stack underflow, ensure you're validating the depth against zero before popping. Also, check if 'AtomicGroupContext' is being correctly initialized for nested calls. This is likely a C-level logic bug rather than a Python-level one.

I corrected the stack depth check and it fixed the atomic grouping issues. I've also added a set of regression tests to Lib/test/test_regex_compat.py. Everything seems stable now. I'm planning to submit a PR for this branch.

Great work. Before you open the PR, double-check that you've included documentation updates for Doc/library/regex.rst and that the code style conforms to PEP 8. Running a final 'python -m test test_regex' one more time wouldn't hurt. Sounds like we're ready for review!

I've updated the documentation in Doc/library/regex.rst and verified that all function docstrings match PEP 257. One final thing: should I expose the new regex flags directly, or should I alias them to re.A, re.I, etc. to maintain total compatibility?

It is standard in CPython to provide the full set of constants. I recommend defining them in the regex module while using 'from re import I, M, S, X as regex_flags' to ensure the values are binary-compatible if possible, though you should avoid namespace pollution.

That makes sense. I'll import the flags from re for the aliases but keep the new regex-specific ones distinct. I've encountered an issue in test_regex.py where Unicode case folding is slightly inconsistent with re's behavior. Any pointers?

Case folding in regex is often tricky because of Unicode versioning. Check your character property tables in Modules/_regex_unicode.c. Are you using the same unicodedata version as the current interpreter?

Ah, I was using hardcoded property tables instead of the library's internal helpers. I'll refactor Modules/_regex_unicode.c to rely on the unicodedata C API to ensure version consistency with the build.
Good catch. Using the built-in unicodedata C API is much more robust. Make sure to update the internal cache initialization as well; that should resolve the inconsistency.
Refactored. The Unicode tests in test_regex now match re. Everything is passing locally on my machine. I'm running the full regression suite again, including Lib/test/test_unicode.py.
The suite is quite extensive. Check for memory leaks using valgrind if you can, especially in the new C extension. Does your regex compiler handle large backreferences correctly?
I haven't explicitly stress-tested deep backreferences yet. I'll add a test case to Lib/test/test_regex_compat.py involving 100+ nested groups just to be safe before submitting the PR.
That is a wise stress test. If the group indexing logic in _regex.c uses a static array instead of dynamic allocation, you might hit an overflow there.
I confirmed that my current implementation uses a fixed size, so I'll switch it to use PyMem_Malloc to allow for arbitrary depth. This will make the module much safer.
Using PyMem_Malloc is the correct approach. Remember to track those allocations in a cleanup block and hook them into the GC if necessary to prevent memory leaks.
I've updated the memory allocation logic. The tests still pass, and the memory footprint is stable even with high recursion limits. I think I'm ready to commit to the feature branch.
Excellent. Make sure you don't have any debug prints remaining in the C code, as they can be quite noisy. Also, double-check your 'setup.py' configuration for the new C module.
Checked, no prints left. setup.py is updated to include _regex.c and _regex_unicode.c in the build process. I'm preparing to open the Pull Request now.
Make sure you include a summary of your benchmarks compared to the re module in the PR description, as reviewers will definitely ask for performance metrics.
I've benchmarked it against re on several standard strings and the results look competitive. I will include those findings in the PR comment.
Sounds great. This regex module is a significant addition to the library. Good luck with the initial review cycle!
Thanks for all the help! I've just pushed the branch and opened the PR on GitHub. Waiting for feedback from the maintainers now.
You're very welcome. It's been a solid process. If the maintainers request changes, you know where to reach me for another pair of eyes.

I received feedback on the PR. The maintainers want me to make sure the new _regex module handles empty matches correctly in cases where the re module currently behaves differently. They referenced a specific edge case in Modules/_regex.c regarding zero-width matches at the end of a string.

That is a classic regex implementation trap. In Modules/_regex.c, ensure that your match state machine correctly updates the search pointer even when the match length is zero. You might need to look at how re.finditer handles these cases to ensure strict compatibility.

I see the issue now. My scan loop inside _regex_match_recursive in Modules/_regex.c uses a post-increment check that skips the zero-width state if it's at the very end of the string buffer. I'm modifying the loop condition to account for that empty match transition.

Good catch. While you are there, double-check that the behavior is consistent for both bytes and unicode patterns. You should verify this by adding a new test case to Lib/test/test_regex.py that specifically targets end-of-string zero-width matches.

I've added the test case in Lib/test/test_regex.py. Running it now triggers a test failure as expected. I'm working on the fix for the loop logic to handle the termination condition gracefully without skipping the empty match.
Make sure that when you apply the fix in _regex.c, you also verify that you are not causing an infinite loop in cases where the regex matches empty strings repeatedly, like in the pattern 'a*'.

Good point. I've added a check to ensure the input pointer advances by at least one character if a zero-width match occurs, mirroring the logic found in Modules/_sre.c. Testing now shows the infinite loop is avoided.
That mirrors the standard library approach perfectly. Are you seeing any performance regressions with this added branch in the hot path of the matcher?

Running the micro-benchmarks with timeit, the impact seems negligible. The branch is only taken in edge cases, and the compiler handles the branch prediction well since it's rarely executed on typical strings.
That sounds optimal. Go ahead and commit those changes to the PR branch. Do you have a plan for updating the documentation for the new module?

I've started drafting the Doc/library/regex.rst file. It needs to reflect the new features while explicitly highlighting where it diverges from the standard re module, specifically regarding the new flags and recursive support.
That is critical. Maintainers are usually sticklers for documentation, especially for library-level modules. Ensure you include examples for the advanced features like possessive quantifiers.
I'll make sure to add a dedicated section for possessive quantifiers and atomic grouping. I am also updating Doc/whatsnew/3.x.rst to mention this as a major addition.
Excellent. Keep the examples in your documentation clear and concise. Have you considered adding a cross-reference to the original issue 2636 in the documentation metadata?

Yes, I included the issue reference at the top of the file. I'm currently running the full suite of tests including Lib/test/test_re.py to ensure I haven't broken any cross-compatibility expectations.
Running the existing re tests against your new implementation is the gold standard for validation. If you pass those, you're in a very strong position for approval.
All tests in Lib/test/test_re.py passed! I'm feeling confident about the stability. I'm pushing the updated documentation and the fix for the zero-width edge case to GitHub now.
Great progress. Once those docs are up and the CI passes, I'd suggest pinging the reviewer on the PR to take another look at the logic improvements.
I've sent the ping. I am also preparing a brief summary of the changes to add to the PR description so the reviewers don't have to hunt through the commits.
That is a very professional move. It makes the reviewer's job much easier and significantly speeds up the final approval process. Let me know when you hear back.

The reviewer just flagged an issue with Modules/_regex.c regarding potential memory leaks when compiled with specific debug flags. They mentioned that the reference counting in the regex_exec function isn't correctly handling instances where the match object initialization fails midway. I need to audit that path.

That is a classic pitfall in CPython extension modules. Check the error handling flow inside regex_exec. Ensure you're calling Py_DECREF on your local variables if the object creation fails before returning NULL. You might need to restructure the cleanup with a goto fail pattern common in Modules/_regex.c.

I've applied the goto fail pattern to the initialization logic in Modules/_regex.c. I'm running a Valgrind check now to confirm. The initial sweep shows the memory leak is gone, but I am seeing a new warning about a potentially uninitialized pointer when the input string is empty.

The empty string case is a notorious edge case for the new regex engine. Check your check_empty_input function in _regex_core.c. You likely need to explicitly initialize your buffer pointer to NULL to avoid those compiler warnings, even if the logic prevents actual access.

Good catch! I initialized the pointer to NULL in _regex_core.c and the compiler warning has disappeared. Running the full test suite again to ensure these changes didn't regress the performance of the non-empty string matches.

Smart move. High-performance string scanning is delicate. Use the timeit module to compare execution times for long-string matching before and after your pointer initialization change. We don't want to incur a performance penalty for that safety.

Performance results are identical, which is a relief. Now, I'm focusing on the Unicode support. The reviewer mentioned that regex.py should correctly handle property lookups like \p{Letter} in line with the new PEP standards.

Python's unicode database is exposed via the unicodedata module. Ensure your regex parser in _regex_core.c properly imports this and caches the property lookups, as doing a lookup for every match iteration will be extremely slow.

I've integrated the caching mechanism using a dictionary lookup for unicode properties. It significantly improves throughput for large regex patterns containing multiple character classes. I'm updating Lib/regex.py to expose these properties as first-class citizens.

Make sure you document that behavior in your Doc/library/regex.rst additions. Users will need to know if they can use custom unicode property names or if they are strictly limited to the standard Unicode version supported by the current build.

I added a note about strict versioning based on the build's unicodedata version. I also added a test case in Lib/test/test_regex.py that uses complex nested unicode properties to verify the parser handles the backslash escapes correctly.

You're covering a lot of ground. How is the compatibility check going with the existing re module flags? Have you verified that regex.IGNORECASE behaves exactly the same as re.IGNORECASE for non-ASCII characters?

That was tricky, but I confirmed that regex.IGNORECASE now uses the fold case implementation from unicodedata to match the expected standard. I've added a table in the documentation to clarify the flag mapping between regex and re.

Having that mapping table is a great user experience improvement. It helps developers transition without hunting through source code. Does the test suite verify this behavior specifically for locales?
Yes, I've added a test case in Lib/test/test_regex.py that switches locales and verifies that the case-insensitive matching remains robust. Everything seems to hold up under stress testing.
You seem to be reaching a stable point. Have you considered the impact on the CPython build system? Does Makefile.pre.in need any changes to include the new _regex module correctly in the build?

I had to update the setup.py to include _regex as an extension module and ensure it links against the shared libraries correctly. It’s compiling fine on Linux, and I’m currently setting up a remote VM to test the Windows build.
Windows builds are often the bottleneck due to how C extensions handle symbol exports. Make sure your PC/build_ext.py configuration explicitly exports the module entry point correctly.

Good call. I added the necessary exports in the Windows-specific configuration file. I'm now pushing these final build system changes to the feature branch. Hopefully, the automated CI will green-light the PR.

The hard work is done. With the unit tests passing, documentation updated, and the build system configured for cross-platform stability, you should be ready for the final merge review. Keep me posted!

I am looking at the CI output for the feature branch, and it seems like the test_regex.py is failing on the Windows x64 build agent. Specifically, I'm seeing a ModuleNotFoundError: No module named '_regex' during the initialization phase.

That error typically points to the build system failing to copy the compiled binary into the expected site-packages directory or the Lib/ folder for the test runner. Check your setup.py script to ensure the _regex extension is being included in the build_ext execution.

You are right. It looks like my modification to setup.py was wrapped in a conditional that was false on Windows. I've updated it to ensure that Modules/_regex/regex.c is included regardless of the host platform.

That makes sense. Ensure you also check PCbuild/pcbuild.sln if you're building via Visual Studio, as it might need an explicit project reference for the new _regex module to ensure it's compiled before the test suite starts.

I've added the project reference to PCbuild/pcbuild.sln, but now I'm getting a linker error: LNK2001: unresolved external symbol PyUnicode_Contains. It seems the regex C extension is missing a dependency on the core Python Unicode headers or libraries.

That function is part of the Unicode API in Python. Verify that you have included the proper header, usually Python.h, and that your module linking configuration includes the python3.lib stub during the build step on Windows.

Adjusted the includes in Modules/_regex/regex.h to ensure Python.h is the first import. The linker error persisted, so I had to explicitly link against python3x.lib in the project properties. That seems to have cleared the LNK2001 errors.
Excellent. Now that the linker is happy, run a clean build. Residual build artifacts in the build/ directory can sometimes cause false positives even after configuration changes.

Cleaned the build directory, and it compiled successfully on the Windows VM! Running test_regex.py now. Wait, I'm getting a segfault in test_case_insensitive_unicode_matching. It looks like memory corruption.
Memory corruption in regex engines usually points to an off-by-one error during string processing or an incorrectly calculated buffer size in Modules/_regex/regex.c when dealing with surrogate pairs.

I debugged the buffer size calculations, and you were right. I was using strlen instead of the custom _regex_string_length function. This caused buffer overflows for non-BMP characters. Fixed that, and the segfault is gone.
Great catch. BMP handling with surrogate pairs has always been a pain in C-level Unicode processing. Are the tests in Lib/test/test_regex.py passing now, or are there still intermittent failures?
They are passing consistently! I also ran the full standard test suite to ensure no regressions in the re module. Everything looks stable across all platforms now.
That is a huge milestone. Have you performed any final cleanup of the code? Sometimes these debugging sessions leave behind temporary print statements or commented-out code in the C sources.
Good call. I just did a thorough code review of Modules/_regex/regex.c and removed all debug macros. The code is looking very clean. I'm ready to open the final pull request.
Before you open the PR, make sure you squash your commits into logical, descriptive units. It makes the code review process much easier for the core developers.
Squashing the commits now. I'll include a detailed summary referencing Issue 2636. I want to make sure the documentation I wrote in Doc/library/regex.rst is also included in the commit set.
Perfect. Once you hit push, verify that the PR title and description follow the standard Python contribution guidelines, referencing the issue number for automatic tracker integration.
The PR has been pushed to the main branch! I'm seeing the CI status turn green on GitHub Actions. It feels great to finally reach this point after months of effort.

Congratulations on getting the regex module into a state ready for merge! It's a significant contribution to the Python standard library. Great job staying persistent through the Windows build issues.

I noticed one final potential issue while reviewing the CI logs. Even though tests pass, the memory usage spikes during the stress tests in Lib/test/test_regex_stress.py. Should I be concerned about this before the maintainers review?

A memory spike is common when dealing with complex regex engines due to backtracking. Check if the recursion depth limit is being respected in Modules/_regex/regex.c. If it's spiking excessively, verify you are freeing the state objects correctly.

You're right. I looked at the state cleanup logic in _regex_free_state. I was missing a call to PyMem_Free on the pattern object cache. Adding that should bring the baseline memory consumption down significantly.
Good spot. Ensure that PyMem_Free is called only after ensuring the cache isn't being referenced by active compiled objects. Race conditions in the GC path can be subtle.
I've added the fix and re-run the stress test. Memory footprint is stable now, even with concurrent compilation tests. I'm going to push these small refinements to the existing PR branch.
Excellent. Pushing those fixes is the right move. Have you verified that these changes don't impact the performance metrics in Tools/scripts/regex_benchmark.py?
I just ran the benchmark script. The overhead is negligible, and some operations are actually faster due to better cache management. I'm feeling confident about this final state.
That is encouraging news. A performance boost is a great bonus. Are there any outstanding stylistic issues flagged by the linter checks? Python core has strict guidelines on C-style indentation.
The linter pointed out a few tabs vs spaces issues in Modules/_regex/regex.c and some missing docstrings. I've corrected them to match PEP 7 standards.
Good work on the PEP 7 compliance. It's often the small things that get caught during the formal review process. Are you ready to request a code review from the module maintainers?
Yes, I've requested a review from Serhiy Storchaka, as he is very familiar with the re module codebase. I hope he has time to look at it soon.
Serhiy is the perfect person for this. He's incredibly thorough and often catches edge cases that even the CI suite misses. Prepare for detailed feedback!
He already commented on the way I handle the flags bitmask. He suggested using the same bitmask logic as Lib/re.py to maintain consistency. That's a clever observation.
That makes perfect sense for interoperability. Implementing that change will make the new regex module feel truly native to the Python ecosystem. Do you need help with that refactor?
I think I've got it. I'm mapping the new flags to the internal structure in _regex_compile_init. It should be a straightforward update, though it requires touching Doc/library/regex.rst again.
Updating the documentation in tandem with the API changes is vital. Make sure to reflect the new flag constants clearly for users who are migrating from the old module.
Documentation is updated. I've also added a 'Migration Guide' section to the docs to make the transition easier for users switching from re to regex.
That's a very thoughtful addition. Documentation is often the biggest hurdle for adoption. You've really put in the extra work here.
I'm relieved. The feedback loop is closing, and the PR seems to be nearing approval. It's been an intense few months but it's been worth it.
It is definitely worth it. You've handled the technical challenges and the collaborative aspects of the Python community beautifully. Best of luck with the final merge!

I just received one last comment from Serhiy on the Modules/_regex.c file. He's concerned that the memory allocation pattern in the unicode processing loop might be vulnerable to buffer overflows with specifically crafted invalid regex strings.

That is a serious catch. The safety of the buffer handling in Modules/_regex.c is paramount, especially since we're dealing with raw string pointers. Have you investigated using PyMem_Calloc to ensure cleaner zero-initialization?

Good suggestion. I am switching from malloc to PyMem_Calloc for the internal pattern structure in the _regex_init_pattern function. I'm also adding bounds checking against the pattern length parameter.

Adding the bounds check is the right move. Even if the logic seems sound, defensive programming at the C level is non-negotiable for CPython contributions. Let's verify the updated test suite afterwards.
I've applied the bounds check, but I'm now seeing a Segfault in Lib/test/test_regex.py when running the fuzzy matching test cases. It seems I miscalculated the buffer offset by one byte.
Off-by-one errors are classic. Check the way you define the terminal NULL character in your buffer allocation. If you are allocating N bytes, ensure you allocate N+1 for the safety break.
Spot on. I was allocating exactly the string length, failing to account for the trailing NULL. Adjusted the size calculation in Modules/_regex.c and the Segfault is gone.
Glad to hear that. Are the tests in Lib/test/test_regex.py passing consistently now, or are there still intermittent failures under high memory pressure?
Everything is green. I ran the full test suite through the valgrind integration, and it reports zero leaks or illegal memory access errors during regex object initialization.
Excellent news. Valgrind passing is a high bar for C extensions. With that cleared, I think you're ready to submit the final diff for the maintainer's sign-off.
I've just pushed the final commit to the branch. I also updated the build configuration in setup.py to include the new extension module, ensuring it compiles across different platforms.
Checking setup.py is a subtle but important detail. Make sure the headers are correctly installed in the Include/ directory so users can interact with the API if needed.
Done. I moved the relevant header declarations to Include/internal/pycore_regex.h to keep the namespace clean and avoid leaking internal definitions to the end-user.
Perfect architecture. By keeping internal definitions isolated in Include/internal/, you minimize the surface area for ABI changes in future Python versions.
Serhiy just gave the final approval on the GitHub thread! He noted that the performance metrics in the docs are well-justified by the underlying optimizations in the regex engine.
That is high praise. You've navigated the entire lifecycle of a core CPython feature, from the initial proposal in issue 2636 to final code review and validation.
It feels surreal. I'm waiting for the merge commit to hit the main branch. Any advice on how to handle the inevitable bug reports once it enters the beta phase?
Be patient and systematic. Use the same issue tracker, request minimal reproducible scripts, and keep a clean changelog. You've built a robust foundation; you'll handle it just fine.
Thanks for all your guidance throughout this process. Your feedback on the memory management and code structure really saved me from some major headaches.
It was my pleasure! You did the heavy lifting. Congratulations on successfully contributing a major, high-performance module to the Python standard library.

I noticed a small regression in Lib/test/test_re.py where unicode property lookups are failing on narrow builds. I should investigate the _regex.c implementation to ensure PyUnicode_Check is handled correctly.
Good catch. Narrow builds often expose issues with surrogate pairs in custom regex engines. Check Modules/_regex.c to see if you are using the correct wide character conversion macros.
I found the culprit: I was using PyUnicode_AS_UNICODE directly which is discouraged. Switching to PyUnicode_AsWideCharString should resolve the memory safety concerns and narrow build errors.
That is a much safer approach. Remember to free the buffer returned by PyUnicode_AsWideCharString to avoid memory leaks during regex compilation.
I have implemented the fix in Modules/_regex.c. I'll run the test suite again. Should I add a dedicated test case in Lib/test/test_regex.py to prevent regression?
Absolutely. Create a test case that uses characters outside the Basic Multilingual Plane to ensure the engine handles high-range unicode correctly on all platforms.
Test passed! The new test case in Lib/test/test_regex.py confirmed the fix for U+1F600 emojis and other non-BMP characters. I feel more confident about the module now.
The confidence boost is well-deserved. Testing against edge cases like non-BMP unicode is exactly the type of rigor expected in core CPython development.
Now that the fix is verified, I'm updating the documentation in Doc/library/regex.rst to clarify the unicode behavior. I want users to know exactly what to expect.
Clear documentation is as important as the code itself. Make sure to explicitly mention the support for surrogate pairs if you've addressed that in the latest build.
I've added the note to the docs. It's really coming together. Do you think I should also expose some internal flags to let power users tune the engine's performance?
Be careful with that. Adding new flags creates a permanent API surface. Only expose them if there is a demonstrated, significant performance gain for common use cases.
That makes sense. I'll keep the API minimal for now and document the current optimizations in the 'Performance' section instead. Less is more when it comes to public APIs.
Exactly. You can always introduce new tuning flags in a future release if the community demands more granular control over the compilation process.
I'm performing one last scan of the codebase for any missed error handling paths. I want to make sure that PyErr_SetString is called in every failure case.
Look closely at the state machine transitions in Modules/_regex.c. If a transition fails, verify that you aren't leaving the GIL in an inconsistent state.
Checked the GIL management. I am holding the GIL for all critical state changes and ensuring that all early exits properly decrement the reference counts for objects.
Excellent. Memory management in extensions is the most common cause of crashes in CPython. It sounds like your module is production-ready.
The merge commit just hit! I can see 'regex' showing up in the build logs. It's official, the new module is part of the standard library now.
Congratulations! Watching your work become part of the Python core is a unique milestone. Take a moment to celebrate this success.

I noticed in the latest build logs for Lib/test/test_regex.py that we have a minor regression in a localized performance test. It seems like the JIT compilation step in _regex.c is slightly slower on 32-bit platforms compared to the baseline.

That is concerning. Check the architecture-specific macros in Modules/_regex.c, particularly around how we handle word-aligned pointers. On 32-bit builds, the address space layout might be causing alignment issues that impact the JIT hot path.

You are right. I found that the buffer allocation for the state machine code didn't account for the stricter alignment requirements on some architectures. I'm adding a PyMem_AlignedAlloc call to ensure we meet the hardware requirements.
Good catch. Once you've implemented the change, run the test suite specifically with PYTHONMALLOC=debug to ensure you aren't introducing any subtle memory leaks during the re-allocation process.

Ran the debug malloc tests and everything looks clean. The memory footprint remains stable, and the JIT performance on the 32-bit build server has returned to expected levels. I'm feeling confident about this fix.
Excellent. Does the fix pass the existing tests in Lib/test/test_regex.py, or do you need to adjust any threshold parameters in the performance benchmarks?

I didn't need to change the thresholds, which is a relief. However, I did notice that the docstrings in the header file Modules/_regex.h were slightly outdated after these changes. I'm updating them to reflect the new alignment behavior.
Keeping documentation in sync with low-level implementation details is crucial. Ensure the Sphinx generator still correctly parses these updated comments for the official Python docs.
Good point. I'll run make doc-check to verify that the documentation builds correctly and that no warnings are generated during the Doc/library/regex.rst compilation.
Wait, did you check the compatibility with re.compile? If someone calls re.compile using our new module's flags, we need to ensure they are handled gracefully rather than raising a hard exception.

I added a wrapper layer in Modules/regexmodule.c that checks for flag compatibility before passing the arguments to the compiled engine. If an unsupported flag is used, it now issues a proper ValueError.
That is the correct approach. It preserves backward compatibility while steering users toward the newer, more robust regex features without breaking existing codebases.
I'm looking at the final test coverage reports, and we are sitting at 98% branch coverage. I want to hit that last 2% in the error-handling paths of the compiled regex parser.
Try creating a test case in Lib/test/test_regex.py that intentionally provides malformed byte strings to trigger those specific branches. That should push your coverage over the final hurdle.
Added a series of negative tests that feed invalid bytecode to the engine. It triggered the final branch, and the error propagation logic held up perfectly under the pressure of the tests.
It seems the module is truly production-ready now. Is there anything left to clean up in the repository before we consider the 'regex' project completely finished?
Just a final cleanup of the build configuration files. I'm removing the temporary debug build targets I created in Makefile.pre.in to keep the repo clean.
Good practice. Don't forget to run a clean build one last time to ensure that no stale objects are lingering in the build directory.
